14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.
135: 
136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
137: 
138: ---
139: 
140: ## 5. FRONTMATTER
141: 
142: Frontmatter is optional for normal project READMEs and recommended for skill or system documentation that should be discoverable.
143: 
144: ```yaml
145: ---
146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:
149:   - "[search phrase]"
150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
153: 
154: Use frontmatter when it improves routing, search or maintenance. Omit it for small human-only documents.
155:

14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.
135: 
136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
137: 
138: ---
139: 
140: ## 5. FRONTMATTER
141: 
142: Frontmatter is optional for normal project READMEs and recommended for skill or system documentation that should be discoverable.
143: 
144: ```yaml
145: ---
146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:
149:   - "[search phrase]"
150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
153: 
154: Use frontmatter when it improves routing, search or maintenance. Omit it for small human-only documents.
155: 
156: ---

# Skill Reference File Templates - AI Agent Skills

Templates for creating reference files in AI agent skills with deep-dive technical guidance.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Location & Naming

**Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`

**Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only

|---------------|-----------------|
| `implementation-workflows.md` | `ImplementationWorkflows.md` (PascalCase) |
| `tool-catalog.md` | `tool_catalog.md` (snake_case) |
| `debugging-guide.md` | `DebuggingGuide.MD` (wrong case) |
| `quick-reference.md` | `quickReference.md` (camelCase) |

```markdown
---
title: [Title]
description: [One-line description - same as intro]
trigger_phrases:

  - "[distinctive phrase two]"
  - "[distinctive phrase three]"
importance_tier: normal
contextType: general
version: 1.0.0.0
---

# [Title]

[1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]

---

\## 1. OVERVIEW
[All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]

```

> **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
> The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.

#### GOOD Intro Structure

```markdown
# Git Commit Workflows

This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.

---

\## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose
Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.

### When to Use
- Creating commits with multiple file changes
- Filtering generated files from commits
- Writing clear commit messages

### Core Principle
Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
```

---

Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
```

| Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |

---

### Reference Body Skeleton

**Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.

# SKILL.md File Templates - Creation Guide

Templates for creating SKILL.md files with proper structure, frontmatter, and required sections.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose of SKILL.md Files

SKILL.md files define AI agent skills - reusable capabilities that extend an agent's functionality for specific domains or workflows. A well-crafted SKILL.md:

- **Triggers automatically** when relevant patterns are detected
- **Guides the agent** through specialized workflows
- **Maintains consistency** across conversations
- **Encodes expertise** in specific domains

### Template Overview

This guide provides **one comprehensive SKILL template** (Section 3) that covers all skill types from simple single-purpose tools to complex multi-mode orchestrators.

**The template is flexible:**
- **Simple skills**: Use required core sections only (WHEN TO USE, SMART ROUTING, HOW IT WORKS, RULES, REFERENCES)
- **Skills with bundled resources**: Say in Section 2 what selects the skill and what it loads first, and put the router in the sibling `ROUTER.md`. Use `references/`, `assets/`, and `scripts/`
- **Multi-mode skills**: Expand WHEN TO USE and HOW IT WORKS sections by mode
- **All skills**: Section 2 (SMART ROUTING) is required: 8 to 12 non-blank lines of plain prose

**Target size**: 800-2000 lines for SKILL.md (<5k words total)

**Examples**:
- Simple: Unit test generator, documentation formatter (no bundled resources)
- Moderate: API client, specialized code reviewer (with references and assets)
- Complex: Workflow orchestrator, document quality pipeline (multi-mode with extensive resources)

### Progressive Disclosure Principle

SKILL.md architecture follows progressive disclosure:

1. **Metadata** (YAML frontmatter) - Always in context (~100 words)
2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill activates (<5k words)
3. **Bundled resources** - Loaded as needed (unlimited size)

**Critical**: Keep SKILL.md <5k words. Move detailed content to `references/`, `scripts/`, or `assets/`.

### Document Type Requirements

**Enforcement Level**: STRICT (SKILL.md files require perfect structure)

**Required Elements**:
- ✅ YAML frontmatter with required fields
- ✅ H1 title with subtitle
- ✅ Numbered H2 sections (ALL CAPS, integers only, never a letter suffix such as `2b.`)
- ✅ Section separators (`---`)
- ✅ No table of contents (forbidden in SKILL.md)

**Quality Targets**:
- Structure: 100/100
- Content quality: High (AI-evaluated)
- Overall: High (human/AI judgment)

---

## 2. FRONTMATTER REQUIREMENTS

### Required Fields

| Field | Required | Format | Example |
|-------|----------|--------|---------|
| `name` | ✅ | hyphen-case | `my-skill-name` |
| `description` | ✅ | Single line, **≤ 130 chars** for skills (≤ 110 for commands), 1,536-char hard cap | `"Handles X when Y occurs"` |
| `allowed-tools` | ✅ | Array: `[Tool1, Tool2]` | `[Read, Write, Edit, Bash]` |
| `version` | ✅ | 4-part X.Y.Z.W | `1.0.0.0` |

> **Hard rules**: not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside the skill's `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects that the dispatch preflight reads.

> **Description budget & trim style**: see [`frontmatter-templates.md` § Description Budget & Trim Style](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md).
> Keep total project descriptions under the ~6,400-character ceiling. This leaves headroom below the 8,000-character auto-discovery limit.
> Drop product and stack lists. Drop marketing prose. Keep the skill name, primary verb, domain noun and mode suffixes (`:auto` or `:confirm`).

```yaml
---
name: sk-example
description: Example workflow skill demonstrating proper frontmatter format with specific capabilities, use cases, and key differentiators for AI agent discovery.
allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep]
version: 1.0.0.0
---
```

- **name**: Must match folder name exactly, hyphen-case only
- **description**: Third-person voice, single line, no `<>` brackets
- **allowed-tools**: Use brackets `[...]`, not comma-separated string
- **hard rules**: Not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects the dispatch preflight reads.

---

**Size Constraints** (package_skill.py validation):
- Max 5000 words (3000 recommended)

- `package_skill.py` fails if `REFERENCES` is missing and no approved combined `SMART ROUTING & REFERENCES` structure exists.

13: # Figma to Code Translation
14: 
15: How to read a Figma design as a reference and build the simplest correct structure from it.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### Purpose
22: 
23: A Figma read, export or MCP pull tells you what the screen should look like and which states it has. It does not tell you which elements to write.
24: 
25: ### When to Use
26: 
27: - Reading a Figma frame before writing code
28: - Translating auto layout, sizing or absolute layers into CSS
29: - Mapping Figma variables and styles to installed tokens
30: - Running the five-pass check against a rendered build
31: - Reporting a Figma-to-code red flag
32: 
33: ### Core Principle
34: 
35: Figma is a reference for code, never its markup. Never copy the layer tree, absolute coordinates, fixed frame sizes or component property sets 1:1 into code.
36: 
37: ### Boundaries
38: 
39: This file does not own:
40: 
41: - **Element choice.** That decision belongs to [`web-markup-and-css.md`](web-markup-and-css.md), and every value comes from the tokens the app installs.
42: - **Shared principles.** The shared principles are in [`frontend-practice.md`](frontend-practice.md). The web layer names the mechanics each app uses.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. WHY FIGMA COMPONENTS LOOK THE WAY THEY DO
47: 
48: Design teams build one Figma component to serve many use cases without creating a new variant for each. That flexibility costs structure:
49: 
50: - **Boolean properties** that show or hide layers, so one button covers icon-left, icon-right and text-only.
51: - **Instance-swap slots** that accept any icon or nested component.
52: - **Nested auto-layout wrapper frames**, added to control padding, alignment or clipping on the canvas.
53: - **Absolutely positioned layers**, so the component stays resizable in the editor without its parts reflowing.
54: - **Fixed frame widths and text boxes with set sizes**, sized for one artboard, often a 375 px phone frame.
55: - **Variants for states** (hover, pressed, focus, disabled) and sizes, because Figma has no pseudo-classes or props.
56: 
57: That structure serves the canvas and the designer. Code usually needs a simpler, more effective structure: fewer elements, normal flow, states from CSS or props, and values from tokens.
58: 
59: ---
60: 
61: ## 3. TRANSLATION TABLE
62: 
63: | Figma construct | Web |
64: |-----------------|-----|
65: | Auto layout, direction | `display: flex` with `flex-direction`, or grid for two axes |
66: | Auto layout spacing between items | `gap` with a spacing token |
67: | Auto layout padding | `padding` with spacing tokens, logical properties |
68: | Hug contents | Intrinsic size: no width set, or `fit-content` |
69: | Fill container | `flex: 1`, or stretch in the parent |
70: | Fixed width or height | `max-width` or a size token, only when the fixed size is intended |
71: | Absolutely positioned layer | Normal flow, a positioned overlay only when the design truly overlays |
72: | Hidden layer or boolean property | Conditional rendering or a prop |
73: | Instance swap | Children or a slot |

19: ## 1. OVERVIEW

23: A Figma read, export or MCP pull tells you what the screen should look like and which states it has. It does not tell you which elements to write.

46: ## 2. WHY FIGMA COMPONENTS LOOK THE WAY THEY DO
47:

50: - **Boolean properties** that show or hide layers, so one button covers icon-left, icon-right and text-only.
51: - **Instance-swap slots** that accept any icon or nested component.
52: - **Nested auto-layout wrapper frames**, added to control padding, alignment or clipping on the canvas.
53: - **Absolutely positioned layers**, so the component stays resizable in the editor without its parts reflowing.
54: - **Fixed frame widths and text boxes with set sizes**, sized for one artboard, often a 375 px phone frame.
55: - **Variants for states** (hover, pressed, focus, disabled) and sizes, because Figma has no pseudo-classes or props.

35:

37: 
38: - **Web mechanics.** The web layer expresses the principles through DOM and CSS. It names the vocabulary and mechanics that implement them, in [web-markup-and-css.md](web-markup-and-css.md).

42: 
43: ## 2. THE ELEVEN PRINCIPLES
44: 
45: 1. **Actions are buttons, and navigation is links.** People get the expected interaction and navigation behavior. See [web structure](web-markup-and-css.md#2-structure-and-semantics).
46: 2. **Every control has a name, a role and a state.** People need to identify a control and understand its current condition. See [web structure](web-markup-and-css.md#2-structure-and-semantics).
47: 3. **Every input has a visible label, and its affordance matches the data.** A visible label stays available after a person starts typing, while the input cue helps them enter the right data. See [web forms](web-markup-and-css.md#3-forms).
48: 4. **Layout follows content flow, siblings have consistent spacing, text containers grow with their text, overlays leave the flow, and content respects device safe areas.** This lets content adapt without clipping or hiding ordinary content. See [web layout](web-markup-and-css.md#4-layout).
49: 5. **Text survives translation and font scaling.** Longer translations and larger system text must remain readable and reachable. See [web responsive rules](web-markup-and-css.md#5-responsive).
50: 6. **Every image has a text-alternative decision and reserved dimensions.** People using assistive technology need the image's meaning, and the layout needs its space before it loads. See [web media](web-markup-and-css.md#6-media).
51: 7. **Values come from installed tokens, and a missing token is reported.** Installed tokens keep values consistent across the app, while a report gives the design system a clear gap to resolve. See [web CSS architecture](web-markup-and-css.md#7-css-architecture).
52: 8. **Figma is a reference, not a code structure.** A design shows intended appearance and states, while the app's own conventions decide its structure. See the [web boundary](web-markup-and-css.md#1-overview) and [Figma to code](figma-to-code.md).
53: 9. **Responsive behavior is checked at narrow, medium and wide widths and under zoom.** These checks expose wrapping, overflow and clipping before release. See [web responsive rules](web-markup-and-css.md#5-responsive).
54: 10. **Assistive-technology checks are part of completion, and non-essential motion respects the user's reduced-motion setting.** They confirm names, order, states and feedback when people do not use the visual layout. See the [web checklist](web-markup-and-css.md#9-pre-completion-checklist).
55: 11. **Text and controls meet the contrast target set by sk-design-fundamentals on every theme the mode supports.** Contrast remains readable in each supported theme. See [web structure](web-markup-and-css.md#2-structure-and-semantics) and [sk-design-fundamentals](../../../sk-design/sk-design-fundamentals/SKILL.md).

60:

120:

13: # Web Accessibility Patterns
14: 
15: Widget contracts, focus handling and browser accessibility preferences for web interfaces.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### Purpose
22: 
23: This file covers widget behavior, focus and browser accessibility preferences. Support summaries use the web-features Baseline classifications and browser-version data.
24: 
25: ### When to Use
26: 
27: - Adding or changing a modal dialog
28: - Mapping a component library's behavior to a widget pattern
29: - Naming controls or moving focus
30: - Adding announcements or honoring browser accessibility preferences
31: - Building a widget pattern or wiring form validation and error messages
32: 
33: ### Boundaries
34: 
35: - Native element choice and baseline semantics: [web-markup-and-css.md](web-markup-and-css.md).
36: - State selectors such as `:focus-visible`: [web-cascade-and-selectors.md](web-cascade-and-selectors.md).
37: - Element and attribute mechanics for dialogs, popovers and forms: [web-elements-and-attributes.md](web-elements-and-attributes.md).
38: 
39: ---
40: 
41: ## 2. MODAL DIALOG CONTRACT
42: 
43: ### A1. Modal dialog
44: 
45: - **Rule:** Use native `<dialog>` with `showModal()` or a component library's documented modal behavior.
46: - **Why:** These mechanisms provide top-layer placement, Escape handling, focus containment and an inert background.
47: - **When not to:** Use a non-modal dialog when the surrounding page must remain interactive.
48: - **Pitfall:** Setting `aria-modal="true"` on an ordinary element hides the rest of the page from assistive technology without making the page inert.
49: - **Support:** Baseline widely available since 2024-09-14 (web-features `dialog`). Chrome 37 / Firefox 98 / Safari 15.4.
50: - **See also:** [WAI-ARIA APG: Dialog (modal)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/)
51: 
52: ---
53: 
54: ## 3. LIBRARY MAPPING
55: 
56: When a component library provides widget roles, state, focus movement or announcements, use that behavior as the source of truth. For hand-written widgets, implement the complete pattern described below.
57: 
58: | Pattern | Integration boundary |
59: |---|---|
60: | Modal dialog | Close through the dialog lifecycle so focus returns to the opener. |
61: | Menu button | Use a disclosure and navigation list for site navigation; a menu role promises menu keyboard behavior. |
62: | Tabs, listbox or combobox | Do not add tabindex values or arrow-key handlers when a component manages roving focus; treat its autocomplete as a combobox and do not redeclare supplied roles. |
63: | Accordion, disclosure or tooltip | Keep expanded state aligned; disabled controls may not receive focus, and a tooltip cannot be the only label. |
64: | Status region, table or grid | Keep the live region mounted before changing its text; set `aria-sort` on the sorted header when needed. |
65: | Focus styling | Keep a visible replacement if an outline is removed. |
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 4. NAMES AND FOCUS
70: 
71: ### A2. Accessible name order
72: 
73: - **Rule:** Prefer `aria-labelledby` that points to visible text, and preserve the order `aria-labelledby`, `aria-label`, host-language label, then `title`.
74: - **Why:** A higher-priority naming source replaces lower-priority sources in the computed accessible name.
75: - **When not to:** Omit ARIA naming attributes when a native label already provides the intended name.
76: - **Pitfall:** An `aria-label` of `Send` replaces visible `Submit` text and can break speech input that uses the visible label.
77: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
78: - **See also:** [MDN: Accessible name calculation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Guides/Accessible_name_calculation)
79: 
80: ### A3. Roving tabindex and active descendant
81: 
82: - **Rule:** Use roving tabindex for items that move DOM focus, and use `aria-activedescendant` when focus stays on a text input.
83: - **Why:** Roving tabindex moves browser focus, while `aria-activedescendant` exposes an active child without moving focus from its owner.
84: - **When not to:** Use neither pattern for ordinary links or buttons that already provide the needed keyboard behavior.
85: - **Pitfall:** The active descendant must reference a rendered element with a stable ID, so virtualized options can leave a dangling reference.
86: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
87: - **See also:** [WAI-ARIA APG: Combobox](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/combobox/)
88: 
89: ### A4. Focus return through the dialog reference
90: 
91: - **Rule:** Close a library-managed overlay through its documented lifecycle so it can restore focus to the opener.
92: - **Why:** The component lifecycle can return focus after the modal leaves the top layer.
93: - **When not to:** Focus a logical successor when the opener no longer exists after the interaction.
94: - **Pitfall:** Removing a dialog through application state can bypass the component lifecycle and leave focus on `body`.
95: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
96: - **See also:** [WAI-ARIA APG: Dialog (modal)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/)
97: 
98: ### A5. Focus-visible styling
99: 
100: - **Rule:** Use `:focus-visible` for browser-selected focus styling and retain a clear keyboard focus indicator.
101: - **Why:** The browser tracks input modality and matches the selector when it determines a focus indicator is needed. Use [CS9](web-cascade-and-selectors.md#cs9-existing-state-selector-contract) for the state-selector contract that applies to focus styling.
102: - **When not to:** Add an explicit focus state when a programmatic focus change must always display a ring.
103: - **Pitfall:** Programmatic focus may not match `:focus-visible`, even when the newly focused container needs an indicator.
104: - **Support:** Baseline widely available since 2024-09-14 (web-features `focus-visible`). Chrome 86 / Firefox 85 / Safari 15.4.
105: - **See also:** [MDN: :focus-visible](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/:focus-visible)
106: 
107: ### A6. Inert background
108: 
109: - **Rule:** Set `inert` on the background while a custom modal is open, and leave the modal subtree interactive.
110: - **Why:** Inert removes descendants from sequential focus and interaction, while `aria-hidden` only changes the accessibility tree.
111: - **When not to:** Do not set `inert` when the surface is a non-modal overlay that leaves the page usable.
112: - **Pitfall:** Applying `inert` to the overlay itself makes its controls unreachable.

115: 
116: ---
117: 
118: ## 5. ANNOUNCEMENTS AND PREFERENCES
119: 
120: ### A7. Live-region timing
121: 
122: - **Rule:** Mount a live-region container before updating its text, set `aria-atomic="true"` when the whole message must be read and reserve assertive announcements for interrupting errors.
123: - **Why:** Assistive technology observes changes to an existing live region and may miss a region created with its first message.
124: - **When not to:** Do not add a live region to content already announced through ordinary navigation or focus movement.
125: - **Pitfall:** Recreating an alert region for each render can repeat the same message or fail to announce it.
126: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
127: - **See also:** [MDN: aria-live](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Reference/Attributes/aria-live)
128: 
129: ### A8. Forced colors
130: 
131: - **Rule:** Use system colors such as `Canvas`, `CanvasText`, `Highlight` and `HighlightText` for essential text, and use borders rather than shadows for boundaries in forced-colors mode.
132: - **Why:** The browser can replace author colors and remove background images when forced colors are active.
133: - **When not to:** Use `forced-color-adjust: none` only when preserving a specific color is necessary to convey meaning.
134: - **Pitfall:** Hard-coded SVG fills and shadow-only borders can disappear from the high-contrast presentation.
135: - **Support:** Baseline widely available since 2025-03-12 (web-features `forced-colors`). Chrome 89 / Firefox 89 / Safari 16.
136: - **See also:** [MDN: forced-colors](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/forced-colors)
137: 
138: ### A9. Reduced motion
139: 
140: - **Rule:** Put optional motion inside `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference` and keep progress feedback available in both modes.
141: - **Why:** The default path remains safe when the preference is unknown or reduced, while the opt-in applies motion only to users who allow it.
142: - **When not to:** Do not add an animation when a state change is already clear without motion.
143: - **Pitfall:** A global animation reset can remove a loading spinner and leave no visible progress cue.
144: - **Support:** Baseline widely available since 2022-07-15 (web-features `prefers-reduced-motion`). Chrome 74 / Firefox 63 / Safari 10.1.
145: - **See also:** [MDN: prefers-reduced-motion](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/prefers-reduced-motion)
146: 
147: ### A10. Contrast, color scheme and transparency preferences
148: 
149: - **Rule:** Set `color-scheme` for supported themes, honor contrast preferences, and treat reduced-transparency styling as a feature-detected enhancement over an opaque baseline.
150: - **Why:** The media preferences expose user display choices, while `color-scheme` lets browser controls adapt to the declared theme.

154:   - `prefers-contrast`: Baseline widely available since 2024-11-30 (web-features `prefers-contrast`). Chrome 96 / Firefox 101 / Safari 14.1.
155:   - `prefers-color-scheme`: Baseline widely available since 2022-07-15 (web-features `prefers-color-scheme`). Chrome 76 / Firefox 67 / Safari 12.1.
156:   - `color-scheme`: Baseline widely available since 2024-08-03 (web-features `color-scheme`). Chrome 98 / Firefox 96 / Safari 13.
157:   - `prefers-reduced-transparency`: Baseline limited availability (web-features `prefers-reduced-transparency`). Chrome 119 / Firefox unsupported / Safari unsupported.

162: ## 6. WIDGET PATTERNS
163: 
164: ### A11. Carousel
165: 
166: - **Rule:** Provide a visible rotation control, pause rotation on hover and focus and set `aria-live="off"` while it rotates.

170: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
171: - **See also:** [WAI-ARIA APG: Carousel](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/carousel/)

173: ### A12. Table and grid
174: 
175: - **Rule:** Use a native table for static data and use `role="grid"` only when the widget implements its full keyboard interaction model.
176: - **Why:** A grid role promises managed focus and keyboard navigation beyond a table's row and column relationships.
177: - **When not to:** Use a grid when users edit, select or navigate cells as an interactive widget.
178: - **Pitfall:** A sortable table needs `aria-sort` on the currently sorted header.
179: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
180: - **See also:** [WAI-ARIA APG: Grid](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/grid/)
181: 
182: ### A13. Menu button
183: 
184: - **Rule:** Pair `aria-haspopup="menu"` and `aria-expanded` with Up or Down to open, Home and End, typeahead, Escape to close and return focus and Tab to close.

187: - **Pitfall:** Applying `role="menu"` to ordinary site navigation changes assistive-technology expectations without supplying menu keyboard behavior.
188: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
189: - **See also:** [WAI-ARIA APG: Menu button](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/menu-button/)
190: 
191: ### A14. Tooltip
192: 
193: - **Rule:** Give supplemental content `role="tooltip"`, associate its trigger through `aria-describedby`, show it on hover and focus and let Escape dismiss it.
194: - **Why:** The described-by relationship makes the tooltip's supplemental text available when the trigger receives focus.
195: - **When not to:** Use a dialog or popover when the content contains interactive controls.
196: - **Pitfall:** A tooltip on a disabled control may never appear, and a tooltip cannot provide the control's only name.
197: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
198: - **See also:** [WAI-ARIA APG: Tooltip](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/tooltip/)
199: 
200: ---
201: 
202: ## 7. FORMS AND VALIDATION
203: 
204: ### A15. Framework validation layers
205: 
206: - **Rule:** For forms handled by a framework validation layer, render app feedback and confirm whether the framework disables native browser validation. Keep native constraint attributes so the framework can read them.
207: - **Why:** A framework may add `novalidate` or otherwise replace browser validation bubbles while still using attributes such as `required` and `min` as validator inputs.
208: - **When not to:** Use browser-native validation when its message UI is the intended path.
209: - **Pitfall:** `setCustomValidity()` does not restore browser validation UI while `novalidate` remains on the form.
210: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
211: - **See also:** [MDN: Constraint validation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Constraint_validation)
212: 
213: ### A16. Error association in library and hand-written fields
214: 
215: - **Rule:** Inside a component library's form-field wrapper, let the library associate its error and hint messages. In a hand-written field, bind the visible message ID and invalid state to the control.
216: - **Why:** A library may add message IDs to the input's `aria-describedby` list and update its `aria-invalid` state. For a hand-written field, give each message an ID, reference it from the control and set the invalid state when validation fails.
217: - **When not to:** Do not add a duplicate `aria-describedby` ID or invalid-state binding when the component already manages both.
218: - **Pitfall:** A library may show an error when a control is invalid and touched or when the form is submitted. A hand-written component that shows errors only when dirty behaves differently.
219: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
220: - **See also:** [WAI: Forms tutorial, notifications](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/notifications/)
221: 
222: ### A17. Error summary and focus on submit
223: 
224: - **Rule:** After a failed submit, focus the first invalid control or an error summary that links to each invalid control.
225: - **Why:** The summary gives assistive technology users one place to review errors and jump to the affected fields.
226: - **When not to:** A single-field form, such as a search box, can keep focus on its field and show the inline error there.
227: - **Pitfall:** After a submit handler marks every control as touched, focus remains on the submit button unless code moves it. Newly rendered error text is not automatically announced.
228: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
229: - **See also:** [WAI: Forms tutorial, notifications](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/notifications/)
230: 
231: ### A18. Async validator pending state
232: 
233: - **Rule:** Block submission while a form is pending as well as when it is invalid. Expose validation progress with `aria-busy` on the field group or a polite status message.
234: - **Why:** An asynchronous validator can leave a form pending while both its valid and invalid states are false.
235: - **When not to:** A form with no async validators needs only the `invalid` check.
236: - **Pitfall:** A submit check that reads only `form.invalid` can run before async validation finishes. A disabled control leaves the tab order and is excluded from the form's aggregate value.
237: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
238: - **See also:** [MDN: Constraint validation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Constraint_validation)

206: - **Rule:** For forms handled by a framework validation layer, render app feedback and confirm whether the framework disables native browser validation. Keep native constraint attributes so the framework can read them.

209: - **Pitfall:** `setCustomValidity()` does not restore browser validation UI while `novalidate` remains on the form.
210: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
211: - **See also:** [MDN: Constraint validation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Constraint_validation)

213: ### A16. Error association in library and hand-written fields
214: 
215: - **Rule:** Inside a component library's form-field wrapper, let the library associate its error and hint messages. In a hand-written field, bind the visible message ID and invalid state to the control.

220: - **See also:** [WAI: Forms tutorial, notifications](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/notifications/)
221:

223:

226: - **When not to:** A single-field form, such as a search box, can keep focus on its field and show the inline error there.

229: - **See also:** [WAI: Forms tutorial, notifications](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/notifications/)

238: - **See also:** [MDN: Constraint validation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Constraint_validation)

13: # Web Cascade and Selectors
14: 
15: How the CSS cascade decides between declarations, and how modern selectors match and weigh.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### Purpose
22: 
23: This file covers cascade order, selector specificity and modern selector behavior, one rule per mechanism.
24: 
25: ### When to Use
26: 
27: - Changing how competing declarations resolve across origin, cascade layers, specificity and source order.
28: - Rewriting a selector that relies on `:is()`, `:where()` or `:has()` matching, or on a specificity calculation.
29: - Adding native nesting or an `@scope` boundary to existing selectors.
30: - Registering a custom property with `@property`.
31: 
32: ### Boundaries
33: 
34: - **Baseline CSS architecture.** The baseline CSS architecture rules remain in [web-markup-and-css.md](web-markup-and-css.md).
35: - **State selectors.** The state selector contract is owned by [web-markup-and-css.md Section 7](web-markup-and-css.md#7-css-architecture), and the visible keyboard focus rule by [web-accessibility-patterns.md A5](web-accessibility-patterns.md#a5-focus-visible-styling).
36: 
37: ---
38: 
39: ## 2. CASCADE AND SPECIFICITY
40: 
41: ### CS1. Cascade decision order
42: 
43: - **Rule:** Resolve competing declarations by origin and importance, layer order, specificity, scope proximity when scoped rules apply, then source order.
44: - **Why:** The cascade compares these criteria in order, so a later rule cannot win by source order when an earlier criterion already decided the result.
45: - **When not to:** Skip the comparison when the declarations do not apply to the same element and property.
46: - **Pitfall:** Normal unlayered declarations outrank normal declarations in named layers, while important declarations reverse layer precedence.
47: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
48: - **See also:** [MDN: CSS cascade](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Cascade)
49: 
50: ### CS2. Global cascade layer order
51: 
52: - **Rule:** Declare the cascade layer order once in a global stylesheet before component styles load.
53: - **Why:** Layer order is established the first time each layer name appears. Component style injection can vary with load order, so per-component layer blocks cannot define a reliable shared order.
54: - **When not to:** Use unlayered styles only when the app deliberately relies on the unlayered precedence boundary.
55: - **Pitfall:** A deeply scoped rule inside a layer loses to an unlayered rule even when its selector looks stronger.
56: - **Support:** Baseline widely available since 2024-09-14 (web-features `cascade-layers`). Chrome 99 / Firefox 97 / Safari 15.4.
57: - **See also:** [MDN: CSS cascade layers (@layer)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@layer)
58: 
59: ### CS3. Specificity arithmetic
60: 
61: - **Rule:** Count IDs, class-like selectors and type selectors in separate specificity columns before changing a selector.
62: - **Why:** IDs add to the first column, classes, attributes and pseudo-classes add to the second, and type selectors and pseudo-elements add to the third. A component-scoping attribute such as `[data-scope]` adds one class-like unit.
63: - **When not to:** Do not raise specificity when the actual conflict comes from origin, importance or cascade layer order.
64: - **Pitfall:** A selector such as `.card[data-scope]` has specificity `0-2-0`, not `0-1-0`.
65: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
66: - **See also:** [MDN: CSS specificity](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Specificity)
67: 
68: ---
69: 
70: ## 3. SELECTOR LOGIC
71: 
72: ### CS4. Zero-specificity and maximum-argument selectors
73: 
74: - **Rule:** Wrap low-priority defaults in `:where()` and use `:is()` when the matching alternatives should share the strongest argument's specificity.
75: - **Why:** `:where()` contributes zero specificity, while `:is()` contributes the specificity of its most specific argument.
76: - **When not to:** Keep a direct class selector when the alternatives would obscure which component states match.
77: - **Pitfall:** Adding a high-specificity selector to one `:is()` alternative raises the specificity of the entire selector.
78: - **Support:** Baseline widely available since 2023-07-21 (web-features `is`). Chrome 88 / Firefox 82 / Safari 14. Baseline widely available since 2023-07-21 (web-features `where`). Chrome 88 / Firefox 82 / Safari 14.
79: - **See also:** [MDN: :is()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/:is)
80: 
81: ### CS5. Narrow relational matching with :has()
82: 
83: - **Rule:** Keep `:has()` selectors narrow and close to the component that owns the matching relationship.
84: - **Why:** The browser reevaluates relational matches as the relevant DOM changes, and a broad ancestor selector can increase style invalidation work.
85: - **When not to:** Prefer an existing direct selector when the relationship is already represented by a simple parent or sibling structure.
86: - **Pitfall:** A broad rule such as `body:has(.is-open)` makes unrelated subtree changes relevant to a page-level selector.
87: - **Support:** Baseline widely available since 2026-06-19 (web-features `has`). Chrome 105 / Firefox 121 / Safari 15.4.
88: - **See also:** [MDN: :has()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/:has)
89: 
90: ---
91: 
92: ## 4. NESTING, SCOPE, PROPERTIES AND STATE
93: 
94: ### CS6. Native nesting and the nesting selector
95: 
96: - **Rule:** Use `&` to make the parent selector explicit inside native CSS nesting.
97: - **Why:** The nesting selector represents the full parent selector, so `&:hover` and `.theme &` express relationships without Sass-style string concatenation.
98: - **When not to:** Keep a selector flat when nesting would hide its reach or increase selector complexity.
99: - **Pitfall:** `&-active` does not append a suffix to a class name as it would in Sass.
100: - **Support:** Baseline widely available since 2026-06-11 (web-features `nesting`). Chrome 120 / Firefox 117 / Safari 17.2.
101: - **See also:** [MDN: Using CSS nesting](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_nesting/Using_CSS_nesting)
102: 
103: ### CS7. Scoped selector boundaries
104: 
105: - **Rule:** Use `@scope` to limit a rule to a component subtree when the required browsers support it.
106: - **Why:** Scoped rules stop at the declared scope boundary, and scope proximity breaks a tie after specificity without changing the selector's specificity.
107: - **When not to:** Use the established component scoping mechanism when a target browser does not support `@scope`.
108: - **Pitfall:** A scope boundary does not prevent unscoped rules from matching the same descendants. In Safari 26.0 through 26.3, rules inside `@scope` do not apply to `<input>` and `<textarea>`; support is complete from 26.4.
109: - **Support:** Baseline newly available since 2026-03-24 (web-features `scope`). Chrome 143 / Firefox 146 / Safari 26.4.
110: - **See also:** [MDN: CSS @scope](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@scope)
111: 
112: ### CS8. Registered custom properties
113: 
114: - **Rule:** Register a custom property with `@property` when its type, inheritance behavior or animation behavior must be explicit.
115: - **Why:** Registration gives the browser a syntax, an `inherits` setting and an initial value, which lets typed values interpolate during animation.
116: - **When not to:** Keep an unregistered property when it only carries an inherited token and needs no typed animation.
117: - **Pitfall:** A registered property with the wrong `inherits` value can stop a theme token from reaching its descendants.
118: - **Support:** Baseline newly available since 2024-07-09 (web-features `registered-custom-properties`). Chrome 85 / Firefox 128 / Safari 16.4.
119: - **See also:** [MDN: CSS @property](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@property)
120: 
121: ### CS9. Existing state selector contract
122: 
123: - **Rule:** Follow the state selector contract in [web-markup-and-css.md Section 7](web-markup-and-css.md#7-css-architecture).
124: - **Why:** The web layer already owns how exposed state reaches CSS selectors, so this file does not define a second state source. See [A5](web-accessibility-patterns.md#a5-focus-visible-styling) for the visible keyboard focus rule.
125: - **When not to:** Use a class for a visual-only state that has no semantic state in the markup.
126: - **Pitfall:** A store-owned `.is-open` class can drift from the expanded state already present on the control.
127: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
128: - **See also:** [MDN: Attribute selectors](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Attribute_selectors)
129: 
130: ---
131: 
132: ## 5. SUPPORT
133:

22:

24: 
25: ### When to Use
26: 
27: - Adding a modal or non-modal overlay
28: - Building disclosure or inert content

33:

41: 
42: ### EA1. Modal and non-modal dialog APIs
43: 
44: - **Rule:** Call `showModal()` for a modal `<dialog>`, and call `show()` only when the page must stay interactive. Treat `closedby` as an enhancement, feature-detect it and keep Escape plus an explicit close button available.
45: - **Why:** `showModal()` places the dialog in the top layer, creates a `::backdrop`, moves focus into the dialog and keeps sequential focus inside it. Escape dispatches a cancel request that closes the dialog unless the handler prevents it. `show()` does not make the rest of the page inert or establish modal focus behavior.
46: - **When not to:** Use `show()` for a non-modal prompt that leaves the surrounding page usable.
47: - **Pitfall:** Setting `aria-modal="true"` after calling `show()` does not create modal focus behavior.
48: - **Support:** Baseline widely available since 2024-09-14 (web-features `dialog`). Chrome 37 / Firefox 98 / Safari 15.4. Baseline limited availability (web-features `dialog-closedby`). Chrome 134 / Firefox 141 / Safari unsupported.
49: - **See also:** [MDN: dialog element](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/dialog)
50: 
51: ### EA2. Popover states and invokers
52: 
53: - **Rule:** Use `popover="auto"` for light-dismiss behavior or `popover="manual"` when the project owns dismissal, and connect declarative controls with `popovertarget`. Feature-detect the `source` option and `popover="hint"`; keep an explicit anchor and an auto or manual popover path.
54: - **Why:** An auto popover joins the browser's auto popover stack and closes on light dismissal. A manual popover stays open until code or an explicit control closes it. `showPopover({ source })` can set the invoker as the implicit anchor for CSS anchor positioning.
55: - **When not to:** Use a dialog when the surface needs modal focus behavior or blocks the page behind it.
56: - **Pitfall:** `popover="hint"` can layer hint popovers without replacing an open auto popover, but its support is not uniform across the declared browsers.

13: # Web Layout and Sizing
14: 
15: The CSS layout mechanics behind stacking, sizing, containers and scrolling.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### Purpose
22: 
23: This file covers stacking contexts, containing blocks, intrinsic sizing, grid tracks, containers and scrolling behavior.
24: 
25: ### When to Use
26: 
27: - Changing how a fixed, sticky or stacked element is positioned.
28: - Sizing flex or grid tracks, or a container query, around intrinsic content.
29: - Handling media ratio, scrollbar space, scroll chaining or viewport height units.
30: - Adding a content-sized control or an intrinsic-size animation.
31: 
32: ### Boundaries
33: 
34: - **Baseline flow and responsive rules.** The baseline flow and responsive rules remain in [web-markup-and-css.md](web-markup-and-css.md).
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. STACKING AND CONTAINING BLOCKS
39: 
40: ### L1. Ancestors that capture fixed positioning
41: 
42: - **Rule:** Keep transforms, filters, perspective, paint or layout containment, relevant `will-change` values and `container-type` off ancestors of viewport-fixed headers or bars.
43: - **Why:** These properties can make an ancestor the containing block for a fixed descendant, so the descendant moves with that ancestor instead of the viewport. Transform, filter and containment behavior is longstanding.
44: - **When not to:** Scope a fixed child to an ancestor only when it is meant to remain fixed inside that component.
45: - **Pitfall:** Adding `will-change: transform` to smooth an ancestor can silently change where a fixed child is positioned.
46: - **Support:** Baseline widely available since 2025-08-14 (web-features `container-queries`). Chrome 105 / Firefox 110 / Safari 16.
47: - **See also:** [MDN: CSS containing block](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Containing_block)
48: 
49: ### L2. Stacking context triggers
50: 
51: - **Rule:** Inspect the ancestor chain for a stacking context before increasing a `z-index` value.
52: - **Why:** A stacking context is painted as one unit, so a descendant cannot out-rank content in a different context. Top-layer elements paint above ordinary stacking contexts. Triggers include:
53:   - the root, positioned elements with non-auto `z-index`, fixed or sticky positioning, and flex or grid items with `z-index`
54:   - opacity below one, blend modes, `transform`, `translate`, `rotate`, `scale`, filters and perspective
55:   - clipping, masks, `isolation: isolate`, `contain: layout`, `contain: paint`, `contain: strict`, `contain: content`, `container-type`, `content-visibility: auto` and `will-change` naming one of these properties
56: - **When not to:** Raise a local `z-index` when the elements already share the same stacking context and the order alone is wrong.
57: - **Pitfall:** An opacity such as `0.999` creates a stacking context, while `isolation: isolate` creates one without changing opacity or clipping paint.
58: - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
59: - **See also:** [MDN: CSS stacking context](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_positioned_layout/Stacking_context)
60: 
61: ### L3. Flow root without clipping

Consolidates intent classification + resource loading into the single Barter-style smart-routing entry point. Detection logic lives in [`stack-detection.md`](shared/references/stack-detection.md); phase lifecycle lives in [`phase-detection.md`](shared/references/phase-detection.md).

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

The smart router maps a detected surface (a declared specific surface, then the SKILLED fallback, then UNKNOWN) plus a classified intent (IMPLEMENTATION / DEBUGGING / VERIFICATION / etc.) to the exact references, assets, and verification commands needed for the active task. Loads only the smallest relevant set so the active context window stays focused.

### When to Use

- After surface detection (see [`stack-detection.md`](shared/references/stack-detection.md)) determines the surface: a declared specific surface, then the SKILLED fallback, then UNKNOWN
- When classifying task wording into the dominant work intent
- When mapping intent to concrete reference paths
- When picking verification commands for the surface

### Core Principle

Routing is a two-stage decision: **surface-first, intent-second**. Surface narrows the resource family: a declared specific surface first, then the SKILLED fallback, then UNKNOWN. Intent narrows the specific files within that family. The detected surface also goes to the compiled front door as `--surface-hint`. When a prompt ties between surfaces, a hinted specific surface leads the bundle. SKILLED already ranks last, so a SKILLED hint changes nothing (`SKILL.md` §3).

### Key Sources

- [`stack-detection.md`](shared/references/stack-detection.md): surface detection (a declared specific surface, then the SKILLED fallback, then UNKNOWN) and SKILLED language sub-detection
- [`phase-detection.md`](shared/references/phase-detection.md) — Phase 1/2/3 lifecycle and phase-specific resource expectations
- `SKILL.md` §2 SMART ROUTING — names the routing authority split and the compiled front door

---

## 2. INTENT MODEL

Intent classification scores task text against weighted keyword signals to pick the dominant work type after surface detection. The vocabulary and weights are authored once, in the `INTENT_SIGNALS` block of §8 MACHINE-READABLE ROUTER; read them there. This section is the human-facing summary of how that block is scored, never a second copy of its keywords.

- Every code task first loads the always-on preamble (stack + phase detection and the universal quality baseline); routing then narrows to the detected surface's slice for the matched intents.
- One dominant intent on one surface loads that surface's slice; two near-tied intents (within the router's ambiguity delta) load both intent sets, deduped by canonical pair.
- A single-surface task never pulls another surface's resources.
- No keyword match, or an `UNKNOWN` surface, falls back to the preamble plus the shared-tier entries its matched intents map — confirm the surface and intent before loading more. See §6 (UNKNOWN FALLBACK) and §7 (LOADING DISCIPLINE) for the full rules.

---

## 10. RELATED RESOURCES

- [`stack-detection.md`](shared/references/stack-detection.md): surface detection (a declared specific surface, then the SKILLED fallback, then UNKNOWN) + SKILLED language sub-detection
- [`phase-detection.md`](shared/references/phase-detection.md) — Phase 1/2/3 lifecycle and per-phase resource loading
- `SKILL.md` §2 SMART ROUTING — names the routing authority split and the compiled front door
- Barter equivalent: `barter/.skilled/skills/sk-code/shared/references/smart-routing.md` (different routing key — git-remote project — but same structural pattern)

---

## 11. MACHINE ROUTER

The hub's detailed routing prose, moved here from `SKILL.md` so the skill body keeps only a short routing summary and a pointer to this file. It sits last, after the stage-two map above, and it declares no map of its own: the `INTENT_SIGNALS` and `RESOURCE_MAP` block in section 8 stays the only replay source.

> **Compiled routing (default-on, flag-gated, additive).** Resolve the mode via the compiled router contract first:
**Session surface hint.** Before you call the front door, run the surface detection in [`stack-detection.md`](shared/references/stack-detection.md) on the session's working directory and the files it is editing.
Then add its result as `--surface-hint <SURFACE>`, for example `--surface-hint SKILLED`.
When the prompt's keywords tie between surfaces, a hinted specific surface leads them.
Workflow modes keep first place, and the targets and the bundle kind stay the same.
`SKILLED` is the fallback surface and always ranks last, so a `SKILLED` hint changes nothing.
With `UNKNOWN`, no hint or a surface the prompt did not match, the `routerPolicy.tieBreak` order applies.

### Surface Router: per-intent leaf sets

Root `ROUTER.md` owns the second-stage `INTENT_SIGNALS` / `RESOURCE_MAP`, while packet-owned resources stay typed through `leaf-manifest.json`.
The hub-level shared controls are declared once, in `ROUTER.md` §8: the `SHARED_CONTROL_RESOURCES` list plus the always-loaded `DEFAULT_RESOURCE` preamble. They resolve on disk but never project as leaves.

39: - **`WEB_CASCADE`** fires on `css cascade layers` or `css specificity conflict`. It loads `references/frontend-practice.md`, `references/web-markup-and-css.md`, and `references/web-cascade-and-selectors.md`.
40: - **`WEB_LAYOUT`** fires on `container query layout` or `css stacking context`. It loads `references/frontend-practice.md`, `references/web-markup-and-css.md`, and `references/web-layout-and-sizing.md`.
41: - **`WEB_A11Y`** fires on `web accessibility pattern`, `focus visible styling`, `keyboard focus`, `broken tab order`, `accessible name`, or `aria live region`. It loads `references/frontend-practice.md`, `references/web-markup-and-css.md`, and `references/web-accessibility-patterns.md`.

43: - **`WEB_I18N`** fires on `right to left layout` or `bidirectional text`. It loads `references/frontend-practice.md`, `references/web-markup-and-css.md`, and `references/web-internationalization.md`.

16: The machine router for [`SKILL.md`](./SKILL.md). The core reference is the default resource; each intent adds the web layer or Figma check it needs.
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: This surface holds the core in `references/frontend-practice.md`, the web layer in `references/web-markup-and-css.md`, six web topic files, and the five-pass Figma check in `references/figma-to-code.md`. Every intent loads the core and the matching web or Figma-to-code layer. Topic files load when the request touches their listed concern.
21: 
22: ### Web Topic Files
23: 
24: | Topic | File | Load when |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Elements and attributes | [web-elements-and-attributes.md](references/web-elements-and-attributes.md) | Adding or changing a dialog, popover, disclosure, form-control attribute, or resource hint |
27: | Cascade and selectors | [web-cascade-and-selectors.md](references/web-cascade-and-selectors.md) | Changing selector reach, cascade layers, specificity, or component style boundaries |
28: | Layout and sizing | [web-layout-and-sizing.md](references/web-layout-and-sizing.md) | Changing stacking, containing blocks, intrinsic sizing, container queries, or scrolling |
29: | Accessibility patterns | [web-accessibility-patterns.md](references/web-accessibility-patterns.md) | Changing a widget pattern, accessible name, focus behavior, live region, browser preference, or form validation and error messaging |
30: | Performance and loading | [web-performance-and-loading.md](references/web-performance-and-loading.md) | Changing vitals, resource loading, image delivery, fonts, or main-thread work |
31: | Internationalization | [web-internationalization.md](references/web-internationalization.md) | Changing locale, direction, bidirectional text, formatting, or translation tolerance |
32:

1. In a fresh clone, run `bash .skilled/skills/sk-git/scripts/worktree-naming.sh provision .` first. It installs the dependencies and builds the spec-kit outputs the checks below load. Without it, `parent-skill-check.cjs` and `ci-skill-root-metadata.cjs` fail on a missing `@spec-kit/shared` build.
2. In a clone, run `git config --local skilled.trustRepoHooks true` before you install the hooks. The hooks run this repository's scripts only in a trusted clone, so without it the commit-time re-mint never fires.
3. Install the git hooks with `bash .skilled/scripts/install-git-hooks.sh`. A commit that stages the hub's routing files then re-mints its activation manifest and copies the manifest to its authored path. Without the hooks, do both by hand after each routing change: run `node .skilled/bin/compiled-route-manifest.cjs refresh --hub sk-code --skill-root .skilled/skills/sk-code`, then copy `.skilled/bin/lib/compiled-routing/013-live-activation/activation/sk-code/manifest.json` over `specs/sk-doc/z_archive/019-skill-routing-refactor/015-router-unification-program/013-live-activation/activation/sk-code/manifest.json`.
4. If you prune `specs/`, keep `specs/sk-doc/z_archive/019-skill-routing-refactor/015-router-unification-program/`, the authored source of compiled routing, and keep the `.opencode/skills` link. Without either one the guard and sync checks fail.

### Remove A Surface

Repeat these steps for each surface you drop. `<mode>` is the folder name of the surface packet.

1. Delete the folder `.skilled/skills/sk-code/<mode>/`.
2. In `.skilled/skills/sk-code/mode-registry.json`, delete the mode's `modes` entry and its name in `extensions.surface-axis.surfaces`. In `.skilled/skills/sk-code/hub-router.json`, delete it from `routerPolicy.tieBreak`, delete its `routerSignals` entry and delete the two `vocabularyClasses` that entry names.
3. Regenerate the leaf manifest with `node .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/generate-leaf-manifest.cjs --write .skilled/skills/sk-code`.
4. Edit section 8 of `.skilled/skills/sk-code/ROUTER.md` by hand, because no command writes it. Delete every `RESOURCE_MAP` path under `<mode>/`, then delete each key left with no paths from both `RESOURCE_MAP` and `INTENT_SIGNALS`. Trim the prose map rows and sections above section 8 that point at the removed packet.
5. Update the surface table and the surface list sentence in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/SKILL.md`, the mode's `surfaceDetection` block in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/mode-registry.json` (`stack-detection.md` section 2 reads it) and the surface lines in the root `README.md`.
6. Delete or adjust the files written for the surface. These are its scenarios under `.skilled/skills/sk-code/manual-testing-playbook/`, with their rows in `manual-testing-playbook.md`, the surface checklist pointers in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-quality/`, the entries in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/feature-catalog/feature-catalog.md` and `.skilled/skills/sk-code/feature-catalog/two-axis-registry-driven-routing/two-axis-registry-driven-routing.md`, which name each live surface, the cases in `.skilled/bin/tests/compiled-route-surface-hint.test.cjs` and the canary cases that name the mode in `.skilled/bin/lib/compiled-routing/009-parent-hub-rollout/001-sk-code/fixtures/canary-cases.v1.json`. After a canary edit, copy that fixture over its authored twin at `specs/sk-doc/z_archive/019-skill-routing-refactor/015-router-unification-program/009-parent-hub-rollout/001-sk-code/fixtures/canary-cases.v1.json`.
7. Run `node .skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-skilled/assets/scripts/verify-doc-claims.cjs` and fix every dead path and stale surface count it lists, including those in this README. Then run `node .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/regenerate-skill-derived.cjs --root .skilled/skills/sk-code --write`, which prunes the dead `key_files`, `source_docs` and entities from the hub's `graph-metadata.json`. The only hand edit left in that file is its `causal_summary`, which names each surface.

# Skill README Template

Use this template for `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/README.md`. It writes a skill README in the same narrative voice the repo root `README.md` and the changelogs use: a one-line human pitch, an at-a-glance table near the top, a value-first overview, then quick start, navigation and a verification close.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

Give a person a fast, honest orientation to a skill before they open `SKILL.md`. The README answers what outcome the skill delivers, when to reach for it, what it does not own and how to navigate its files. `SKILL.md` stays the runtime instruction surface. The README is the front door a person reads.

### Identity Guidance (Purpose First)

The identity of a skill is the outcome it delivers. State that outcome in one plain sentence before naming tools.
Describe CLIs, commands, routing paths and reference files only after the outcome.
A README that opens with a tool name has not stated its identity.

The mcp-obsidian README states the outcome first: it makes AI use inside Obsidian effective.
It names the CLIs and MCP server later as delivery surfaces.
Repeat the outcome in the frontmatter description and the pitch.
The description supports a quick scan. The pitch opens the full README.

### Usage

Copy the fillable scaffold in Section 6 into `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/README.md`, then replace every placeholder with current behavior taken from the skill's real files. Keep the numbered ALL-CAPS section headers, the house style and the validator both require them. Drop any section that does not earn its place and renumber the rest.

### Template Focus

The README gives people a human entry point, current capabilities and a clear route to supporting files. This template provides:

- A one-line pitch in a blockquote right after the H1, stating the outcome before any tool name.
- An identity guidance block that puts the delivered outcome ahead of the tooling.
- A capability section pattern for a skill's headline strengths, modeled on the pilot's Plugin Knowledge Layer.
- A dedicated HVR enforcement section with the banned forms and the scripted checks.
- Versioning conventions and a validation checklist that matches the pilot's gates.

---

## 2. SECTION MODEL

A skill README uses numbered ALL-CAPS H2 sections with `---` dividers between them. The default order:

| # | Section | Purpose | Keep When |
|---|---------|---------|-----------|
| 1 | AT A GLANCE | Four-row table a reader scans in five seconds | Always |
| 2 | OVERVIEW | What the skill is and what the reader gets first, then the optional problem narrative | Always (required by the validator) |
| 3 | QUICK START | The fastest path to a first result | Skill has commands, scripts or a workflow |
| 4 | HOW IT WORKS | The main workflow in prose, with a small Mermaid diagram for multi-step flows | Skill has non-obvious behavior worth explaining |
| 5 | INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION | When to use it, plus how it hands off to sibling skills | Readers can confuse it with a neighbor |
| 6 | TROUBLESHOOTING | The failure modes operators actually hit | Predictable issues exist |
| 7 | FAQ | The two to five questions readers keep asking | High-value answers exist |
| 8 | VERIFICATION | How you know the skill works | Skill ships a playbook or validation command |
| 9 | RELATED DOCUMENTS | Stable links out, `SKILL.md` first | Always when links exist |

`OVERVIEW` is the one required section. Its normalized name must appear as a numbered header so the validator finds it. Every other section is optional. A small utility skill might run four sections (AT A GLANCE, OVERVIEW, QUICK START, RELATED DOCUMENTS). A large orchestrator might run all nine. Match the count to the skill. Never pad to hit a number.

Inside OVERVIEW, start with `### What It Does`. Say what the skill is and what the reader gets.
Add up to two optional subsections after it.
Use `### Why This Skill Exists` only to name a current reader problem.
Add the capability section below when it earns a table.

### Capability Section Pattern

When a skill has a headline strength, add a named capability section after What It Does.
Use one or two short sentences to say why the strength matters.
Use an analogy only when it clarifies the mechanism.
Name the section after its domain and add one table row per capability.
State the file or data the skill can operate on.
Avoid marketing claims. The prose explains why the capability matters. The table states what it does.

```markdown
### The Plugin Knowledge Layer

| Plugin | What the skill knows how to operate |
|---|---|
| **Beancount Ledger** | append and patch balanced transactions in the structured `.beancount` ledger |
| **Obsidian Tables** | edit `columns`, `rows` and `views` inside `.table.md` JSON payloads |
```

---

## 3. WRITING RULES

- Apply the [Prose Clarity Checklist](../../references/skill/creation-workflow.md#prose-clarity-checklist) to README prose.
- State the outcome before the tooling. The pitch and the identity guidance name what the reader gets. The tool names follow as the means.
- Open OVERVIEW with what the skill is and what the reader gets.
- Use `### Why This Skill Exists` only to explain a current reader problem.
- Add a short context hook after the blockquote only when it helps the reader. Keep AT A GLANCE as the first numbered section.
- Carry the explanation in prose. Reach for a table only when 4 or more parallel items need a lookup grid (skill relationships, CLI flags, a comparison).
- Use semantic emoji only (✅ ❌ ⚠️ 🔒 🚨) for rules and status markers. Decorative section emoji never: that register belongs to the repository front-page README, while a skill README keeps the technical formatting.
- A short, concrete analogy can carry an abstract mechanism better than adjectives (the repo root README uses "like a lab notebook for software"). Use one only where it clarifies, never as decoration.
- Put the AT A GLANCE table first. Four rows, one line each, no prose cells.
- Name the canonical command or entry point in OVERVIEW or QUICK START so a reader knows where to start.
- Link to real files under `references/`, `assets/`, `scripts/`, `feature-catalog/` or `manual-testing-playbook/`. Verify each path resolves.
- State the expected output for every command you show, so a reader can tell success from failure.
- Be honest about boundaries and trade-offs. If the skill does not own something, say which skill does.
- Keep `SKILL.md` as the runtime surface. The README explains why and how to navigate. It does not restate long reference files.
- Follow the Human Voice Rules. Section 4 lists the banned forms and the scripted checks. It links the full ruleset.
- Vary subsection counts rather than defaulting to three.
- Document current behavior. Keep spec history out of the README.
- Use stable paths and commands. Update the README, its version and its changelog entry when behavior changes.

---

## 4. HVR ENFORCEMENT

Every README this template produces must pass the Human Voice Rules. The full ruleset lives at [`hvr-rules.md`](../../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).

### Banned Forms

The banned forms are: em dashes (U+2014), semicolons (U+003B), Oxford commas (a comma before the final and or or in a list), the hard-blocker words listed below and forced three-item groups.

### Scripted Checks

Run the checks below from the skill root, with the README path as the argument. Each command must return zero matches. The punctuation checks use hex escapes on purpose: the commands stay clean of the characters they enforce.

```bash
rg -n '\x{2014}' README.md
rg -n '\x{3B}' README.md
rg -n ',\s+(and|or)\b' README.md
rg -n '\b(delve|embark|realm|tapestry|illuminate|unveil|elucidate|abyss|revolutionise|game-changer|groundbreaking|cutting-edge|ever-evolving|shed light|dive deep|leverage|foster|nurture|resonate|empower|disrupt|curate|harness|elevate|robust|seamless|holistic|synergy|unpack|landscape|ecosystem|journey|paradigm|enlightening|esteemed|remarkable|skyrocket|skyrocketing|utilize|utilizing)\b' README.md
# Context-dependent words: landscape, ecosystem, journey, unlock, navigating
# Banned as metaphor, allowed in literal use. Judge each hit in context.
```

The word check lists the hard blockers. A hit inside a code sample or a quoted command is exempt. A hit in prose is a violation. Context-dependent words from the full ruleset are banned as metaphor and allowed in literal use. Judge each hit in context.
